items.why: Answerable, but the broad negative wording is less discriminating than asking about the explicit action.
The intended referent is recoverable, but “gives the message” is less natural than “declared the message.”
Clearly distinguishes the group credited with defeating all four from the individual who killed the last one.
A clear pronoun-resolution question that distinguishes the officer from the man of God.
Clearly tests whether the old prophet or his sons performs the action.
Precisely distinguishes the parties to the first covenant from those in the second.
The sequence is explicit and the competing event occurs earlier in the account.
The stated reason is explicit, though the priests’ simultaneous action makes the causal distinction somewhat subtle.
The expected next action is explicit, but the question’s phrasing is stiff.
Clearly tests the men’s final decision against an option they explicitly reject.
The passage clearly orders two killings at Gob and names both killers.
“The news” is vague and the question does not identify the content that was reported.
Clearly distinguishes the king issuing the command from the man he orders seized.
A direct and well-resolved subject-object distinction between Uzziah and Azariah.
Clearly distinguishes which child was planned for today and which for tomorrow.
The instructor is explicitly named and is readily distinguished from Uzziah’s father.
The reply is explicit, but “he” and “any” make the answer less self-contained than ideal.
The refusal and its reason are explicit, complete, and contrasted with a plausible misreading.
The immediate pre-departure action is clearly stated and distinct from the earlier meal.
The action sequence is explicit, though asking what a singular “king” does requires identifying Ben-Hadad from the opening phrase.
Clearly identifies the current giver despite King David’s prior ownership of the weapons.
The ordered group is explicit and distinct from the body that previously heard the case.
The purpose is explicit, though “take” is slightly unnatural and Amaziah’s death is related context rather than a competing purpose.
Clearly distinguishes the direct commanders from the officials who organized the muster.
The victim is clear despite the nearby mention of the prophet who equipped him.
Directly identifies the trampled gate officer and cleanly excludes the king.
The duty assignment is explicit, but the long passage and similar company descriptions increase processing burden.
The letter heading clearly distinguishes its writer from its recipient.
A clear rescue scene that strongly distinguishes the attacker killed from David, the intended victim.
Clearly contrasts the men’s new plan after recognizing wrongdoing with their earlier concealment.
Paul’s quoted instruction explicitly assigns the message to the young man, not Paul.
The immediately preceding event is explicit and distinct from an earlier stage of the mission.
The referent is recoverable, but “Whose love of soil explains” is awkward and interpretive.
Clearly identifies the first child eaten from the speaker’s account and distinguishes the two women.
Clearly distinguishes the man who actually intercedes from the king who requests prayer.
The complete set of peoples God helped Uzziah oppose is explicitly listed.
The sequence clearly distinguishes the first destination, the prophet’s city, from the later tomb.
The hidden child is explicitly identified and clearly distinguished from his dead father.
The passage explicitly links the city’s calm to Athaliah’s death, though the rejoicing is a nearby plausible cause.
Clearly distinguishes the two recipients of the order from the soldiers they must assemble.
Clearly tests the perceived attackers against the king believed to have hired them.
The master-servant wording supports the king as referent, though resolving the insult requires inference.
The quoted claim clearly makes the man of God the one to be brought back to eat and drink.
The passage directly connects Paul’s prolonged speech with his intended departure.
The contrast with the cavalry is clear, but “the soldiers” can sound as though it includes the cavalry.
The plural pronouns clearly refer to the seven sons who were attacked, not the possessed man.
“On the items’ arrival” is unnatural and obscures the simple result of contact with the cloths.
The plot explicitly assigns the task of bringing Paul to the commander, not the council.
The immediate next action is explicit and distinct from the later valuation.
The command explicitly targets followers, but the woman is also subsequently put to death, making the wording easy to misread.
Her reason for going is explicitly the noise, while seeing the king occurs only after she arrives.
The answer is textually stated, but the ambush logically also depends on Paul being brought out, making the distinction unstable.
The warning is directly addressed to the man of God and clearly distinguished from the old prophet speaking.
The prophecy explicitly names Josiah as the future agent and distinguishes him from Jeroboam.
